# Part A — Multiple Choice

### Question 1 — ETC location {#w10-mc01}
The electron-transport chain is embedded primarily in the:

- **A.** outer mitochondrial membrane
- **B.** plasma membrane of animal cells
- **C.** inner mitochondrial membrane
- **D.** nuclear envelope

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: C.**
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w10-mc01 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Proton pumping requires respiratory proteins to span the membrane that separates the matrix from the intermembrane space. That is the inner mitochondrial membrane. Placing the ETC in the outer membrane or freely in the matrix would not match the compartment arrangement used in the guide.

The location matters because electron transport must be connected to a gradient across a membrane. Respiratory proteins in the inner mitochondrial membrane move protons from the matrix side to the intermembrane-space side. ATP synthase in that same membrane can then use their return. The outer membrane does not define the proton barrier described here, and the animal plasma membrane and nuclear envelope are not the locations of this mitochondrial system. Remember the functional arrangement, not just the name: inner membrane separates the two compartments whose proton difference is used to make ATP.

**Review:** [Week 10 study guide](../study-guides/week10-etc-oxidative-phosphorylation.qmd).
:::

### Question 2 — Matrix {#w10-mc02}
Which process takes place in the mitochondrial matrix?

- **A.** proton accumulation during ETC activity
- **B.** glycogen storage only
- **C.** extracellular signaling
- **D.** pyruvate oxidation and the CAC

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: D.**
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w10-mc02 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The matrix is the compartment where pyruvate oxidation and the CAC supply reduced carriers. Proton accumulation occurs on the other side of the inner membrane, in the intermembrane space. Distinguishing production of carriers from accumulation of protons resolves the location question.

The matrix is the compartment enclosed by the inner mitochondrial membrane. Pyruvate is delivered there for PDH processing, and the CAC machinery operates there to generate reduced carriers and the other products studied in Week 9. Proton accumulation during respiratory pumping is on the opposite side of the inner membrane, in the intermembrane space, so that option reverses the relevant geography. Glycogen storage and extracellular signaling are not the matrix processes asked about. Distinguishing soluble pathway location from the membrane and its two sides makes the respiratory sequence easier to follow.

**Review:** [Week 10 study guide](../study-guides/week10-etc-oxidative-phosphorylation.qmd).
:::

### Question 3 — Cristae {#w10-mc03}
Cristae primarily increase:

- **A.** nuclear volume
- **B.** inner-membrane surface area for respiratory proteins
- **C.** DNA replication rate
- **D.** glucose concentration in cytosol

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: B.**
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w10-mc03 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Cristae are folds of the inner membrane, so their direct structural effect is to provide more membrane area. That area accommodates the respiratory machinery and ATP synthase. Increasing nuclear volume or DNA replication is not the function being illustrated.

Cristae are folds of the inner mitochondrial membrane. Folding provides more membrane surface on which respiratory proteins can be organized, so their significance is connected to electron transport and ATP synthesis. The answer is not that the folds increase nuclear volume or directly raise cytosolic glucose concentration. Those options concern different structures or processes. The course also associates more extensive cristae with respiratory activity, but the immediate structural effect being tested is increased inner-membrane area. Start with what the folds are made of, then connect their geometry to the proteins located there.

**Review:** [Week 10 study guide](../study-guides/week10-etc-oxidative-phosphorylation.qmd).
:::

### Question 4 — NADH electrons {#w10-mc04}
NADH carries:

- **A.** 1 electron
- **B.** no electrons
- **C.** 3 electrons
- **D.** 2 electrons

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: D.**
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w10-mc04 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
NADH is the reduced carrier that transfers an electron pair. This is why it is described as carrying two electrons rather than one. The one-electron transfer comparison belongs to cytochromes later in the chain.

NADH is the reduced form of the NAD carrier and carries a pair of reducing electrons in the course's accounting. When it donates that pair, it is oxidized back to NAD+. Do not infer the electron number simply by counting the H in its name. The comparison in this week is between two-electron transfer by NADH and the one-electron steps of carriers such as cytochromes. Recognizing those different transfer sizes explains why the chain needs suitable intermediate carriers; it is not a sequence in which every participant must move the same number at once.

**Review:** [Week 10 study guide](../study-guides/week10-etc-oxidative-phosphorylation.qmd).
:::

### Question 5 — FADH2 electrons {#w10-mc05}
FADH2 is important because it can participate in transfers involving:

- **A.** only protons and no electrons
- **B.** 1 or 2 electrons
- **C.** only 1 electron
- **D.** only 2 electrons

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: B.**
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w10-mc05 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Fully reduced FADH2 holds two electrons, but flavin carriers can participate in one- or two-electron transfer steps. The question asks about that transfer flexibility. It does not mean that a fully reduced FADH2 molecule sometimes contains only one electron.

Distinguish how many electrons the fully reduced carrier holds from how many can move in an individual step. Fully reduced FADH2 holds two electrons, but flavin chemistry permits one- or two-electron transfers. Thus the answer involving one or two describes flexibility, not uncertainty about whether reduced FADH2 sometimes contains only one electron in this comparison. The proton-only choice ignores the redox role, while either only-one or only-two removes the flexibility emphasized by the lecture. This property helps connect carriers that handle electron pairs with carriers that handle single electrons.

**Review:** [Week 10 study guide](../study-guides/week10-etc-oxidative-phosphorylation.qmd).
:::

### Question 6 — Cytochrome {#w10-mc06}
A cytochrome transfers:

- **A.** ATP
- **B.** 1 electron at a time
- **C.** 4 electrons at a time
- **D.** 2 electrons at a time

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: B.**
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w10-mc06 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
A cytochrome's heme iron changes oxidation state by accepting or donating one electron per step. This distinguishes its transfer behavior from NADH's electron-pair transfer. Cytochromes do not carry ATP molecules along the chain.

The relevant change occurs in the cytochrome's heme iron. Switching between Fe3+ and Fe2+ corresponds to accepting or donating one electron, so a cytochrome transfer is counted one electron at a time. This should not be confused with the two-electron contribution represented by NADH. ATP is a different chemical product, not the cargo transferred between cytochromes. The one-electron answer follows from the oxidation-state change of the metal center rather than from a claim that the overall respiratory pathway uses only one electron in total.

**Review:** [Week 10 study guide](../study-guides/week10-etc-oxidative-phosphorylation.qmd).
:::

### Question 7 — Why FAD matters {#w10-mc07}
The ability of FAD/FADH2 to handle one or two electrons is useful because:

- **A.** it can bridge carriers that move electron pairs and carriers that move single electrons
- **B.** it replaces oxygen
- **C.** it pumps protons through ATP synthase
- **D.** it directly phosphorylates ADP

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.**
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w10-mc07 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The chain must connect donors that provide electron pairs with carriers that transfer single electrons. Flavin's one-/two-electron flexibility makes that connection possible. It is an electron-transfer role, not direct ADP phosphorylation or replacement of oxygen.

The chain must connect donors and acceptors with different transfer behavior. NADH transfers an electron pair, whereas a cytochrome handles one electron at a time. A carrier capable of one- or two-electron steps can connect those kinds of transfer without requiring every component to behave identically. That is the bridging function being tested. It does not make FAD a replacement for oxygen as the final acceptor, a proton channel in ATP synthase, or a direct phosphate donor to ADP. Keep the electron-transfer role distinct from the later use of the proton gradient.

**Review:** [Week 10 study guide](../study-guides/week10-etc-oxidative-phosphorylation.qmd).
:::

### Question 8 — Final electron acceptor {#w10-mc08}
The final electron acceptor in oxidative phosphorylation is:

- **A.** CO2
- **B.** O2
- **C.** NAD+
- **D.** FAD

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: B.**
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w10-mc08 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Follow the chain to its endpoint: oxygen accepts electrons at Complex IV and is reduced to water. NADH is an upstream donor, not the terminal acceptor. CO2 is produced in carbon oxidation but is not the final electron sink of this chain.

At the end of the chain, electrons must be passed to an acceptor rather than accumulating indefinitely in the carriers. In this respiratory system, Complex IV transfers them to oxygen. This terminal transfer permits continued upstream electron flow and the energy-conserving pumping coupled to it. NAD+ and FAD are important carrier forms, but they are not the final sink named in this question. CO2 is a carbon-oxidation product from the earlier pathways, not the terminal acceptor. This distinction also explains why loss of oxygen eventually compromises oxidative ATP production.

**Review:** [Week 10 study guide](../study-guides/week10-etc-oxidative-phosphorylation.qmd).
:::

### Question 9 — Energy conservation {#w10-mc09}
As electrons flow down the ETC, released free energy is used directly to:

- **A.** phosphorylate ADP
- **B.** reduce pyruvate to lactate
- **C.** synthesize glucose
- **D.** pump protons across the inner membrane

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: D.**
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w10-mc09 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The immediate energy-conserving event is movement of H+ across the inner membrane. ATP synthase subsequently uses the stored gradient to form ATP. Conflating these two stages would incorrectly make electron transport itself a direct phosphate transfer to ADP.

Pay attention to **directly**. The respiratory complexes use part of the free energy released by electron transfer to move protons across the inner membrane. This creates the electrochemical gradient. ATP synthesis occurs in a linked but subsequent energy-conversion process when protons return through ATP synthase. The ETC therefore does not directly add phosphate to ADP in the way a substrate-level phosphorylation does. Glucose synthesis and lactate formation belong to other pathway functions. The correct answer identifies the intermediate energy store that connects electron flow to ATP production.

**Review:** [Week 10 study guide](../study-guides/week10-etc-oxidative-phosphorylation.qmd).
:::

### Question 10 — Complex I {#w10-mc10}
Complex I:

- **A.** is ATP synthase
- **B.** is located in the outer membrane
- **C.** pumps protons
- **D.** never accepts electrons

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: C.**
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w10-mc10 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Complex I receives NADH-derived electrons and couples electron transfer to proton pumping. Its role belongs to the inner-membrane respiratory chain. ATP synthase is a separate machine that uses the resulting gradient rather than being Complex I.

Complex I belongs to the electron-transport chain in the inner mitochondrial membrane. In the NADH-linked route discussed here, electron entry is associated with energy-conserving proton pumping. Its pumping role places it alongside Complexes III and IV, rather than with the non-pumping Complex II. ATP synthase is a different machine that uses proton return instead of performing this electron-entry role. The outer-membrane location and claim that Complex I never accepts electrons are therefore incompatible with its place in the respiratory sequence. Separate electron transport, proton pumping, and ATP synthesis when assigning functions.

**Review:** [Week 10 study guide](../study-guides/week10-etc-oxidative-phosphorylation.qmd).
:::

### Question 11 — Complex II {#w10-mc11}
Which complex does **not** pump protons?

- **A.** IV
- **B.** I
- **C.** III
- **D.** II

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: D.**
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w10-mc11 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Complex II transfers electrons into the respiratory chain but does not pump protons. Complexes I, III and IV are the pumps emphasized in the course. Participation in electron transport therefore does not automatically imply proton pumping.

Do not assume that every numbered respiratory complex performs both electron transfer and proton pumping. Complex II provides an electron-entry route associated with succinate oxidation and FAD-linked transfer, but it does not pump protons. Complexes I, III, and IV are the pumps identified in the course. This distinction also explains why FADH2-linked entry supports less proton pumping than NADH-linked entry: it bypasses the pumping contribution at Complex I. Complex II is still functionally important even though its role does not include moving protons across the membrane.

**Review:** [Week 10 study guide](../study-guides/week10-etc-oxidative-phosphorylation.qmd).
:::

### Question 12 — Complex IV {#w10-mc12}
Complex IV is especially important because it:

- **A.** converts glucose to glycogen
- **B.** produces NADH in glycolysis
- **C.** makes pyruvate
- **D.** transfers electrons to oxygen

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: D.**
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w10-mc12 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Complex IV completes electron transfer to oxygen, allowing the chain to continue accepting upstream electrons. Oxygen combines with electrons and protons to form water. The complex is not the site of glycolytic NADH production or pyruvate formation.

Locate Complex IV at the terminal end of respiratory electron transfer. Its defining role in this question is passing electrons to oxygen, allowing the chain to continue discharging electrons from upstream carriers. It is also among the proton-pumping complexes, but the distinctive answer offered here concerns the final acceptor. Making pyruvate and NADH in glycolysis occurs in an earlier cytosolic pathway, while glycogen synthesis is a storage process. Matching a complex to its position and recipient is more reliable than selecting any familiar metabolic function.

**Review:** [Week 10 study guide](../study-guides/week10-etc-oxidative-phosphorylation.qmd).
:::

### Question 13 — Proton pumping direction {#w10-mc13}
During electron transport, protons are pumped:

- **A.** from nucleus to cytosol
- **B.** out of the cell
- **C.** from matrix to intermembrane space
- **D.** from intermembrane space to matrix

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: C.**
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w10-mc13 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Pumping stores energy by moving H+ out of the matrix into the intermembrane space. Return through ATP synthase runs in the opposite direction. The question asks about the energy-investing pumping direction, not the gradient-driven return.

Draw the inner membrane with matrix on one side and intermembrane space on the other. Respiratory pumping moves H+ **out of the matrix into the intermembrane space**. This builds the gradient that stores some of the energy from electron transfer. Proton return through ATP synthase goes in the opposite direction during ATP synthesis, which explains the tempting reversed option. The nucleus and the exterior of the cell are not the two sides of this membrane. Always distinguish the gradient-building pumping arrow from the gradient-using return arrow.

**Review:** [Week 10 study guide](../study-guides/week10-etc-oxidative-phosphorylation.qmd).
:::

### Question 14 — Highest H+ concentration {#w10-mc14}
During active respiration, H+ concentration is higher in the:

- **A.** intermembrane space
- **B.** matrix
- **C.** mitochondrial DNA
- **D.** nucleus

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.**
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w10-mc14 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The respiratory complexes move protons from the matrix to the intermembrane space, producing the higher H+ concentration on that side. This difference is part of the stored electrochemical gradient. A region's name alone is not enough; use the direction of pumping to infer its concentration.

Use the pumping direction to derive the answer rather than memorizing it independently. Complexes I, III, and IV move protons from the matrix to the intermembrane space, making the intermembrane-space side higher in H+ concentration in the respiring model. Protons can then return toward the matrix through ATP synthase. The question asks for a compartment containing a higher concentration, not a molecule such as mitochondrial DNA. The matrix option reverses the distribution produced by pumping. This concentration difference is one component of the proton-motive force, not its entire definition.

**Review:** [Week 10 study guide](../study-guides/week10-etc-oxidative-phosphorylation.qmd).
:::

### Question 15 — Proton-motive force {#w10-mc15}
The proton-motive force is:

- **A.** only a chemical concentration gradient
- **B.** an electrochemical H+ gradient
- **C.** the same as NADH concentration
- **D.** ATP hydrolysis energy only

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: B.**
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w10-mc15 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Protons carry charge as well as contributing to concentration differences. The proton-motive force therefore includes an electrical component and a chemical, or pH, component. Calling it only a concentration gradient leaves out part of the driving force.

The prefix electrochemical signals two contributions. There is a chemical difference because H+ concentrations differ across the membrane, and an electrical difference because pumping separates charge. Both contribute to the tendency of protons to return toward the matrix in the respiratory arrangement shown in the course. Naming only the concentration gradient therefore leaves the answer incomplete. NADH supplies reducing equivalents upstream, but its concentration is not itself the proton-motive force. Likewise, ATP hydrolysis is not the definition of the gradient used during oxidative ATP synthesis.

**Review:** [Week 10 study guide](../study-guides/week10-etc-oxidative-phosphorylation.qmd).
:::

### Question 16 — Chemiosmosis {#w10-mc16}
Chemiosmotic coupling links:

- **A.** DNA replication to transcription
- **B.** proton gradient formation to ATP synthesis
- **C.** CO2 production to lactate formation
- **D.** glycolysis directly to glycogen synthesis

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: B.**
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w10-mc16 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Chemiosmotic coupling uses a gradient as the link between electron transport and ATP formation. Respiratory complexes build it, and ATP synthase uses proton return down it. The two processes are connected without electrons directly phosphorylating ADP.

Follow the energy through its intermediate form. Electron transfer supports proton pumping, pumping establishes an electrochemical difference, and proton return through ATP synthase is coupled to formation of ATP. Chemiosmotic coupling refers to that use of the membrane-associated proton gradient to connect the two processes. It is not simply a direct collision between a reduced carrier and ADP. The alternatives involving DNA, glycogen, or lactate name other biological relationships but omit the proton gradient central to this mechanism. The correct answer identifies what links energy conservation to ATP formation.

**Review:** [Week 10 study guide](../study-guides/week10-etc-oxidative-phosphorylation.qmd).
:::

### Question 17 — ATP synthase F0 {#w10-mc17}
The F0 region of ATP synthase is:

- **A.** a DNA-binding protein
- **B.** a soluble glycolytic enzyme
- **C.** the final electron acceptor
- **D.** membrane embedded and involved in proton flow

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: D.**
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w10-mc17 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Fo is the membrane-embedded region through which proton movement is coupled to rotor motion. Its position fits the requirement to cross the inner membrane. The catalytic ATP-forming head is F1, not Fo.

ATP synthase spans a functional boundary between proton movement in the membrane and catalysis on the matrix side. Its F0 region is membrane embedded and participates in the proton-flow and rotary mechanism. The F1 head contains the catalytic sites discussed in the following question. Distinguishing those regions prevents assigning ADP-binding chemistry and membrane proton passage to the same structural description. F0 is not a soluble glycolytic enzyme, a DNA-binding protein, or oxygen's replacement as an electron acceptor. Its role is part of coupling proton return to the movement that drives catalytic changes.

**Review:** [Week 10 study guide](../study-guides/week10-etc-oxidative-phosphorylation.qmd).
:::

### Question 18 — ATP synthase F1 {#w10-mc18}
The F1 region contains:

- **A.** catalytic sites for ATP formation
- **B.** mitochondrial DNA
- **C.** cytochrome c only
- **D.** GLUT2

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.**
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w10-mc18 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
F1 projects into the matrix and contains the catalytic sites involved in ATP synthesis. Fo supplies the membrane-associated proton-driven mechanism. Distinguishing these regions separates chemical catalysis from the route used by protons.

The F1 region is the catalytic head in which the binding-change cycle produces and releases ATP from ADP and Pi. It responds to rotation of the internal shaft generated by proton movement through the membrane-associated part of the enzyme. Thus the catalytic region and proton-flow region perform complementary jobs. Mitochondrial DNA is not the catalytic component, GLUT2 is a glucose transporter from the liver discussion, and cytochrome c is an electron carrier rather than the ATP-forming head. Use the F0/F1 distinction to connect structure to function.

**Review:** [Week 10 study guide](../study-guides/week10-etc-oxidative-phosphorylation.qmd).
:::

### Question 19 — Rotation {#w10-mc19}
Proton flow through ATP synthase drives rotation of:

- **A.** all αβ dimers as a rigid wheel
- **B.** internal rotor components including the central γ shaft
- **C.** the entire mitochondrion
- **D.** Complex IV

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: B.**
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w10-mc19 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The moving component includes the rotor and central gamma shaft. Its rotation changes the shapes of catalytic sites in the stationary head. The entire mitochondrion or all alpha-beta dimers do not rotate together as a rigid unit.

The rotation described is internal to ATP synthase. Proton flow drives rotor movement, including the central γ shaft. As that shaft changes its orientation relative to the catalytic head, the αβ units change conformation. The head should not be pictured as three catalytic units simply spinning together as a rigid wheel. Nor does the whole mitochondrion or Complex IV rotate to make ATP. The question tests how mechanical movement is transmitted to catalytic shape changes, so identifying both what rotates and what responds is essential.

**Review:** [Week 10 study guide](../study-guides/week10-etc-oxidative-phosphorylation.qmd).
:::

### Question 20 — αβ dimers {#w10-mc20}
The αβ catalytic units of ATP synthase primarily:

- **A.** hydrolyze glucose
- **B.** carry oxygen
- **C.** remain chemically unchanged and do nothing
- **D.** change conformation as the central shaft rotates

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: D.**
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w10-mc20 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The catalytic units respond to the rotating central shaft by changing conformation. Those changes alter substrate binding, ATP formation and release. Their role is therefore neither passive nor the transport of oxygen.

Stationary does not mean inactive or unchanging. The αβ catalytic units remain in the head but change their conformations as the central shaft rotates. Those different conformations support binding ADP and Pi, favoring ATP formation, and releasing ATP. The option saying they do nothing overlooks the very changes responsible for catalysis. Hydrolyzing glucose and carrying oxygen are unrelated to their role in this machine. The important distinction is between large-scale rotation of the rotor and changes in shape within the catalytic units that respond to that rotation.

**Review:** [Week 10 study guide](../study-guides/week10-etc-oxidative-phosphorylation.qmd).
:::

### Question 21 — Loose state {#w10-mc21}
In the loose state, the catalytic site mainly:

- **A.** oxidizes NADH directly
- **B.** releases oxygen
- **C.** binds ADP and Pi
- **D.** pumps H+

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: C.**
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w10-mc21 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The Loose state holds ADP and inorganic phosphate at a catalytic site. Tight and Open perform the subsequent formation and release roles in the simplified sequence. Proton pumping occurs elsewhere and is not the direct task of this state.

Use the sequence **bind → form → release** to distinguish the three conformations. The loose state holds ADP and inorganic phosphate so that the substrates are available in the catalytic site. The tight state is associated with ATP formation, and the open state with release. Loose therefore does not mean that the site has no meaningful interaction with its substrates. Proton movement drives the overall rotary mechanism in the membrane-associated region, while NADH oxidation occurs in the respiratory chain. Neither is the direct task of this catalytic binding state.

**Review:** [Week 10 study guide](../study-guides/week10-etc-oxidative-phosphorylation.qmd).
:::

### Question 22 — Tight state {#w10-mc22}
In the tight state:

- **A.** oxygen is generated
- **B.** FADH2 is synthesized
- **C.** ATP formation is favored
- **D.** ATP is expelled from the mitochondrion

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: C.**
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w10-mc22 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The Tight state positions bound ADP and Pi so ATP formation is favored. ATP release is associated with the Open state that follows. The catalytic state does not make oxygen or reduced electron carriers.

After ADP and Pi are held at the catalytic site, the tight conformation favors ATP formation in the lecture's binding-change model. This is distinct from the open state, which allows the product to leave. ATP formation within the head should also be distinguished from transport of ATP out of the matrix, which requires a membrane transporter. The oxygen and FADH2 options refer to redox chemistry rather than this catalytic-state sequence. Locate tight between substrate binding and product release to understand its role rather than treating the three labels as interchangeable names.

**Review:** [Week 10 study guide](../study-guides/week10-etc-oxidative-phosphorylation.qmd).
:::

### Question 23 — Open state {#w10-mc23}
The open state is associated especially with:

- **A.** CO2 fixation
- **B.** ATP release
- **C.** pyruvate oxidation
- **D.** proton pumping by Complex I

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: B.**
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w10-mc23 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Opening lowers affinity for the nucleotide, allowing ATP to leave the catalytic site. This is part of completing a catalytic cycle rather than starting a respiratory-chain reaction. The same site can then bind substrates again as its conformation changes.

ATP must be released for the catalytic site to complete its cycle and become available for another round. The open conformation is associated with that release in the course's loose–tight–open description. Formation alone is not the whole process: a product retained indefinitely would not provide useful continued output. CO2 fixation, pyruvate oxidation, and Complex I pumping belong to other reactions or structures. Also distinguish release from the ATP-synthase catalytic site from export across the inner membrane; they are separate events even though both contribute to delivering ATP for cellular use.

**Review:** [Week 10 study guide](../study-guides/week10-etc-oxidative-phosphorylation.qmd).
:::

### Question 24 — ATP substrates {#w10-mc24}
ATP synthase uses:

- **A.** AMP + pyrophosphate
- **B.** glucose + oxygen
- **C.** ADP + Pi
- **D.** NADH + FADH2

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: C.**
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w10-mc24 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The molecules being chemically combined are ADP and inorganic phosphate. NADH and FADH2 supply electrons upstream, while the gradient supplies the driving energy. These roles are important, but they do not make the carriers the chemical substrates of ATP synthase.

Separate the chemical building materials from the source of driving energy. ATP synthase forms ATP using **ADP and inorganic phosphate**, while the proton-motive force powers the coupled process. NADH and FADH2 are upstream electron donors, not the two chemical substrates joined at the ATP-forming site. Glucose and oxygen describe the wider context of respiration rather than this immediate reaction. The AMP-plus-pyrophosphate alternative also does not match the substrate pair specified in the course. Naming the immediate reactants keeps the enzyme reaction distinct from the full respiratory pathway.

**Review:** [Week 10 study guide](../study-guides/week10-etc-oxidative-phosphorylation.qmd).
:::

### Question 25 — ADP/ATP transport {#w10-mc25}
ATP made in the matrix leaves mainly through:

- **A.** nuclear pores
- **B.** a specific adenine nucleotide transporter
- **C.** GLUT2
- **D.** free diffusion through the inner membrane

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: B.**
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w10-mc25 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The selective inner membrane does not allow newly made ATP to diffuse out freely. A specific nucleotide transport system exchanges matrix ATP for incoming ADP. This transport role differs from ATP synthase's role in catalyzing ATP formation.

The inner membrane is selective, so ATP made on the matrix side cannot simply be assumed to diffuse out freely. Adenine-nucleotide transport links ATP export with ADP entry, helping connect mitochondrial synthesis to cellular use. This transporter is distinct from ATP synthase: synthesis and export are different tasks. GLUT2 transports glucose in the liver discussion and is not an ATP exporter, while nuclear pores cross a different boundary. The correct answer follows from recognizing both where ATP is produced and which membrane must be crossed to make it available outside the matrix.

**Review:** [Week 10 study guide](../study-guides/week10-etc-oxidative-phosphorylation.qmd).
:::

### Question 26 — FADH2 yield {#w10-mc26}
Why does FADH2-linked electron transfer support less proton pumping than NADH?

- **A.** FADH2 carries no electrons.
- **B.** FADH2 blocks Complex IV.
- **C.** FADH2 enters through Complex II and bypasses proton-pumping Complex I.
- **D.** FADH2 consumes oxygen before the ETC.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: C.**
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w10-mc26 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
For the succinate/Complex II route described here, electrons enter after Complex I and therefore miss its proton-pumping contribution. Complexes III and IV can still participate downstream. The lower yield reflects the entry point, not an absence of electrons in FADH2.

Compare the entry routes rather than the total electron content alone. NADH-linked transfer includes the proton-pumping contribution of Complex I. The FADH2/succinate-linked route enters through Complex II, which transfers electrons but does not pump protons, and therefore bypasses that contribution. Downstream electron transfer can still reach the remaining pumping complexes. The lower pumping support does not mean FADH2 contains no electrons or blocks Complex IV. No precise ATP-per-carrier factor is needed to answer: the different route explains why less gradient energy is conserved per corresponding entry in this comparison.

**Review:** [Week 10 study guide](../study-guides/week10-etc-oxidative-phosphorylation.qmd).
:::

### Question 27 — Uncoupler {#w10-mc27}
An uncoupler allows:

- **A.** proton return without ATP synthase
- **B.** glucose to enter mitochondria directly
- **C.** ATP synthesis without a proton gradient
- **D.** cytochromes to carry two ATP each

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.**
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w10-mc27 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
An uncoupler provides a proton-return route that bypasses ATP synthase. It therefore weakens the link between electron transport and ATP capture. It does not supply a way to make ATP without a gradient.

An uncoupler provides a way for protons to return across the inner membrane without their return being captured by ATP synthase. Electron transport may continue transferring energy into pumping, but the gradient is dissipated through the bypass. The word uncoupler therefore refers to weakening the link between oxidation and ATP production, not creating ATP without an energy source. It does not turn cytochromes into ATP carriers or transport glucose directly into the pathway. Identify the bypass around ATP synthase to understand why ATP yield falls despite continued upstream activity.

**Review:** [Week 10 study guide](../study-guides/week10-etc-oxidative-phosphorylation.qmd).
:::

### Question 28 — Uncoupling consequence {#w10-mc28}
If the proton gradient is dissipated while electron transport continues, more energy is released as:

- **A.** heat
- **B.** glycogen
- **C.** DNA
- **D.** CO2 only

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.**
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w10-mc28 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
If protons return without driving ATP synthase, less gradient energy is captured in ATP. More of the energy is dissipated as heat. This is a change in energy partition, not conversion of the gradient into DNA or glycogen.

Under coupled conditions, some energy from electron transport is conserved in the gradient and then captured in ATP. If that gradient is dissipated without ATP-synthase capture, more of the energy is dispersed as heat. The condition that electron transport continues is important: the question is not describing complete cessation of fuel oxidation. Glycogen and DNA would require biosynthetic processes not specified here, and CO2 is a carbon product rather than the form in which the uncoupled energy is released. The answer concerns energy partition, not a new carbon pathway.

**Review:** [Week 10 study guide](../study-guides/week10-etc-oxidative-phosphorylation.qmd).
:::

### Question 29 — Thermogenin location {#w10-mc29}
Thermogenin is found in the:

- **A.** inner mitochondrial membrane of brown adipose tissue
- **B.** nucleus of white adipocytes
- **C.** mitochondrial matrix as a soluble enzyme
- **D.** plasma membrane of red blood cells

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.**
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w10-mc29 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Thermogenin must span the inner mitochondrial membrane to provide an alternative route across the proton barrier. In brown adipose tissue, this arrangement supports heat production. A soluble matrix location would not provide that membrane-crossing route.

Thermogenin must be in the membrane across which the relevant proton gradient exists. In the course example, it is an inner-mitochondrial-membrane protein in brown adipose tissue. That position allows it to provide a proton-return route that bypasses ATP synthase. A freely soluble matrix enzyme would not span the barrier needed for this function, and a nuclear or unrelated plasma-membrane location would not give access to the mitochondrial gradient. Connect its position to its mechanism rather than memorizing brown fat without understanding why the inner membrane matters.

**Review:** [Week 10 study guide](../study-guides/week10-etc-oxidative-phosphorylation.qmd).
:::

### Question 30 — Thermogenin function {#w10-mc30}
Thermogenin:

- **A.** converts NADH to glucose
- **B.** blocks electron transport completely
- **C.** allows H+ to return toward the matrix without ATP synthesis
- **D.** increases ATP production by preventing H+ movement

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: C.**
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w10-mc30 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
UCP1 permits protons to return toward the matrix without producing ATP through ATP synthase. That dissipates gradient energy as heat while fuel oxidation can continue. It is therefore an uncoupler, not simply an agent that stops all electron transport.

Thermogenin, also called UCP1, allows proton return toward the matrix without coupling that return to ATP synthesis. The effect is less capture of gradient energy as ATP and greater heat production. It does not simply prevent all proton movement; allowing the bypass is its crucial function. Nor is it equivalent to a complete block of the electron-transport chain. The respiratory machinery can continue consuming fuel and oxygen while the energy is partitioned differently. The correct option identifies the proton route responsible for that change, rather than assigning glucose synthesis or total respiratory inhibition to the protein.

**Review:** [Week 10 study guide](../study-guides/week10-etc-oxidative-phosphorylation.qmd).
:::

### Question 31 {#w10-mc31}

Which answer addresses BOTH ATP-synthesis substrates and their access to the matrix?

- **A.** NADH and CO2 freely diffuse to ATP synthase as its chemical substrates.
- **B.** Pi is made from oxygen and requires no transport.
- **C.** ADP and Pi are supplied by inner-membrane transport proteins.
- **D.** Only ADP is required, and the membrane has no effect on entry.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: C.** ADP and Pi are supplied by inner-membrane transport proteins.

Lecture 10:20 names ADP and Pi and explicitly states that they enter through transport proteins. Naming ATP synthase alone does not answer the transport part.

**Related objectives:** W10-07
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w10-mc31 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The question has two requirements: identify ADP and Pi, then explain how they reach the matrix. Inner-membrane transport proteins provide their access. Naming ATP synthase answers the catalysis part of the process, not the substrate-supply requirement.

The question has two requirements, and the correct option answers both. ADP and Pi are the immediate chemical substrates for ATP formation. They must also reach the matrix side of a selective inner membrane, so transport proteins are required. Naming ATP synthase alone would explain neither how both substrates arrive nor why free diffusion is an inadequate assumption. NADH provides reducing equivalents upstream and CO2 is a carbon product; they do not replace ADP and phosphate. The main learning objective is transport-dependent access, not memorization of additional carrier names beyond the course's stated requirement.

**Review:** [Week 10 study guide](../study-guides/week10-etc-oxidative-phosphorylation.qmd).
:::

### Question 32 {#w10-mc32}

Which description separates the rotary and stationary components of ATP synthase?

- **A.** The rotor/γ shaft turns while the αβ dimers change conformation without rotating as a rigid head.
- **B.** All αβ dimers rotate together while γ remains immobile.
- **C.** The rotor is a freely soluble enzyme in the cytosol.
- **D.** No component moves or changes conformation during ATP synthesis.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.** The rotor/γ shaft turns while the αβ dimers change conformation without rotating as a rigid head.

The lecture's rotational-catalysis explanation links proton movement to shaft rotation and conformational changes in the stationary catalytic head.

**Related objectives:** W10-08
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w10-mc32 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Separate rotation from conformational change. The rotor and gamma shaft move; the alpha-beta units stay in place but cycle through different catalytic shapes. Describing the whole catalytic head as a spinning wheel would obscure that mechanical-to-chemical coupling.

Imagine the central shaft turning relative to the catalytic head rather than the entire assembly spinning together. Proton movement powers the rotor and γ shaft. The αβ units remain positioned in the head but respond by changing conformation, progressing through the functional states needed to bind substrates, form ATP, and release it. Reversing the moving and stationary roles produces the wrong mechanism. A motionless enzyme or a freely soluble cytosolic rotor likewise cannot explain the membrane-coupled process. The distinction makes clear how mechanical rotation can drive chemical changes at stationary catalytic sites.

**Review:** [Week 10 study guide](../study-guides/week10-etc-oxidative-phosphorylation.qmd).
:::

### Question 33 {#w10-mc33}

Which label set correctly describes the four mitochondrial regions?

- **A.** Outer membrane; intermembrane space; cristae-bearing inner membrane; matrix inside the inner membrane.
- **B.** Outer membrane; nucleus; cytosol; cristae outside the cell.
- **C.** Matrix; endoplasmic reticulum; Golgi apparatus; intercellular space.
- **D.** One membrane surrounding an undivided matrix with no intermembrane space.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.** Outer membrane; intermembrane space; cristae-bearing inner membrane; matrix inside the inner membrane.

The relative positions matter for proton pumping: matrix to intermembrane space across the inner membrane.

**Related objectives:** W10-01
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w10-mc33 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Work from outside inward: outer membrane, intermembrane space, inner membrane and matrix. Cristae belong to the inner membrane. This arrangement explains which barrier protons cross and why matrix and intermembrane-space labels cannot be interchanged.

Place the regions from outside inward: outer membrane, intermembrane space, inner membrane, then matrix enclosed by the inner membrane. Cristae are folds of that inner membrane, not structures outside the cell. This arrangement gives respiratory pumping two distinct sides: protons leave the matrix and accumulate toward the intermembrane space. ATP synthase uses return in the opposite direction. A one-membrane diagram would erase the intermembrane space and confuse the course's compartmental explanation. The incorrect alternatives substitute unrelated organelles or locations instead of describing the mitochondrial structure required by the mechanism.

**Review:** [Week 10 study guide](../study-guides/week10-etc-oxidative-phosphorylation.qmd).
:::

### Question 34 {#w10-mc34}

Why is “FADH2 carries one electron” an incomplete interpretation of the lecture?

- **A.** FADH2 must always donate four electrons simultaneously.
- **B.** Only cytochromes can ever be reduced.
- **C.** FADH2 carries no electrons and only transports ATP.
- **D.** Fully reduced FADH2 holds two electrons; the carrier can transfer one or two at a time.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: D.** Fully reduced FADH2 holds two electrons; the carrier can transfer one or two at a time.

The distinction is between electron content of the reduced carrier and the possible size of an individual transfer step.

**Related objectives:** W10-02,W10-03
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w10-mc34 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Electron content and transfer-step size are different quantities. Fully reduced FADH2 holds two electrons, yet flavin chemistry can support single-electron transfers. Reading the lecture's flexibility statement as a one-electron total loses that distinction.

The apparent contradiction disappears when capacity and transfer size are separated. Fully reduced FADH2 represents a two-electron-reduced carrier. The flavin system can nevertheless participate in steps transferring one electron or two. Saying only that it carries one electron mistakes one possible transfer step for the electron content of the fully reduced form. The lecture emphasizes this flexibility because some partners transfer pairs and others, such as cytochromes, operate in single-electron steps. Neither four-electron donation nor ATP transport is the role being described. State both facts rather than forcing a single transfer-size label onto every aspect of the carrier.

**Review:** [Week 10 study guide](../study-guides/week10-etc-oxidative-phosphorylation.qmd).
:::

### Question 35 {#w10-mc35}

With thermogenin active, what is the expected energy partition relative to fully coupled respiration?

- **A.** Less ATP captured per fuel oxidized and more heat as protons bypass ATP synthase.
- **B.** No fuel oxidation can occur under any condition.
- **C.** No heat because the proton gradient is never dissipated.
- **D.** More ATP because every proton must pass through ATP synthase.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.** Less ATP captured per fuel oxidized and more heat as protons bypass ATP synthase.

UCP1 provides a route for proton return without ATP-synthase capture; it does not mean that all electron transport must stop.

**Related objectives:** W10-09,W11-01
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w10-mc35 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The comparison is ATP captured per amount of fuel oxidized. Thermogenin lets part of the proton return bypass ATP synthase, lowering that capture efficiency and increasing heat release. It does not require a complete shutdown of respiratory electron flow.

Compare the fate of the same kind of respiratory energy under two arrangements. With effective coupling, proton return through ATP synthase supports ATP formation. With thermogenin active, a greater share of proton return bypasses that enzyme, so less energy is captured as ATP per fuel oxidized and more is dissipated as heat. This is not a claim that all respiration stops. It also does not mean every proton must now use ATP synthase; the opposite route has been added. The correct answer links the altered energy partition to the specific bypass mechanism.

**Review:** [Week 10 study guide](../study-guides/week10-etc-oxidative-phosphorylation.qmd).
:::

# Part B — Every Learning Objective

Answer each prompt before opening its model answer. The source sheet supplies the objective; the task underneath makes the required components explicit.

### Objective W10-01 — Mitochondrial structure {#w10-lo01}

**Original objective:** Be clear on mitochondrial structure

Name the four regions, place the ETC, ATP synthase, proton accumulation and PDH/CAC, and explain why cristae matter.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The outer membrane surrounds the organelle. The intermembrane space is between the membranes and is the side to which respiratory complexes pump H+. The inner membrane is highly selective, forms cristae and contains the ETC and ATP synthase. The matrix lies inside the inner membrane and contains the PDH/CAC machinery. Cristae provide membrane area for respiratory proteins; the lecture links denser cristae with high respiratory activity. See the coverage page's source note about the conflicting wording on slide 10:3.

**Source:** Week 10 objectives, item 1; Lecture 10:4–10:6; Alberts Ch. 14.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w10-lo01 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Use membrane boundaries to place each function. PDH and CAC supply carriers from the matrix; inner-membrane proteins transfer electrons and move protons into the intermembrane space. Cristae increase the area available for that membrane machinery, explaining their association with respiratory activity.

Build the structure before adding the pathway arrows. The outer membrane encloses the organelle; the intermembrane space lies between the membranes; the inner membrane folds into cristae; and the matrix is inside that inner boundary. Put PDH/CAC in the matrix and ETC proteins plus ATP synthase in the inner membrane. The intermembrane-space side is where respiratory pumping accumulates H+ relative to the matrix.

Now connect structure to function. A selective inner membrane helps maintain the electrochemical difference, while cristae provide more surface area for the respiratory proteins. Proton pumping and return have meaning only when the sides are correctly labeled. The model answer and coverage page already flag the source wording conflict on slide 10:3; this explanation follows the documented course interpretation rather than silently rewriting the source. Do not confuse membrane folding with enlargement of the nucleus or with a new compartment outside the mitochondrion.

**Review:** [Week 10 study guide](../study-guides/week10-etc-oxidative-phosphorylation.qmd).
:::

### Objective W10-02 — One- and two-electron carriers {#w10-lo02}

**Original objective:** Be clear on how many electrons NADH and FADH2 carry and understand the importance of FADH2 being able to donate and accept either 1 or 2 electrons at a time

Explain the electron capacity of NADH and FADH2 AND why the one-/two-electron distinction matters.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
NADH carries two electrons and transfers a pair. Fully reduced FADH2 also holds two electrons, but the flavin carrier can undergo one- or two-electron transfer steps. That flexibility bridges two-electron donors and one-electron carriers such as cytochromes. “One or two at a time” describes transfer flexibility, not that fully reduced FADH2 contains only one electron.

**Source:** Week 10 objectives, item 2; Lecture 10:7; Tutorial 6.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w10-lo02 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
State electron capacity before explaining transfer behavior. Both fully reduced carriers contain two electrons, but flavin can connect pair-transfer chemistry with single-electron steps. That is why merely saying FADH2 carries one electron is not a complete account of its role.

Answer the electron-content question first. NADH carries two electrons and transfers them as a pair in this account. Fully reduced FADH2 also represents two electrons. Then answer the transfer-flexibility question: the flavin system can participate in one- or two-electron steps, unlike a description restricted to pair transfer alone.

This flexibility is useful because the electron-transport system includes carriers with different transfer behavior. A pair-donating carrier and a one-electron carrier such as a cytochrome need compatible intermediate transfer chemistry. The answer should not claim that fully reduced FADH2 contains only one electron, nor that every individual transfer must involve two. Keeping capacity separate from step size resolves the common confusion. It also prevents incorrectly concluding that FADH2-linked respiration yields less ATP simply because the reduced carrier holds fewer electrons; the different entry route is the relevant comparison elsewhere in this week.

**Review:** [Week 10 study guide](../study-guides/week10-etc-oxidative-phosphorylation.qmd).
:::

### Objective W10-03 — Cytochromes {#w10-lo03}

**Original objective:** Be clear that cytochromes carry 1 electron at a time

How many electrons does a cytochrome transfer per step, and what part changes oxidation state?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Cytochromes transfer **one electron at a time**. Their heme iron cycles between Fe3+ and Fe2+ as it accepts or donates an electron. Do not assign the two-electron transfer behavior of NADH to a single cytochrome step.

**Source:** Week 10 objectives, item 3; Lecture 10:8.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w10-lo03 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The heme iron supplies the redox change underlying cytochrome electron transfer. A change between Fe3+ and Fe2+ corresponds to one electron gained or lost. This makes the one-electron answer a mechanistic statement, not just a number to memorize.

The molecular basis of the one-electron rule is the heme iron's oxidation-state cycle. Acceptance of one electron changes Fe3+ to Fe2+; donation returns Fe2+ to Fe3+. Each such change corresponds to a single electron, so the cytochrome can alternate between reduced and oxidized states while passing electrons along.

Contrast that with NADH's pair transfer rather than assuming all carriers have identical behavior. The chain's overall transfer of reducing equivalents can involve multiple one-electron events even when an upstream donor supplies a pair. This is why flavin transfer flexibility is useful in the course's explanation. A cytochrome is not carrying ATP or moving four electrons in a single iron-state transition. State the number, the changing component, and the direction of the Fe3+/Fe2+ changes to make the answer mechanistic.

**Review:** [Week 10 study guide](../study-guides/week10-etc-oxidative-phosphorylation.qmd).
:::

### Objective W10-04 — Conserving electron-transfer energy {#w10-lo04}

**Original objective:** Be clear that the potential energy conserved as electrons are moving down the electron transport chain is used to pump protons

Explain what electron-transfer energy is used for directly, and distinguish that from ATP formation.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Stepwise electron transfer toward oxygen releases free energy. Respiratory complexes conserve part of it by pumping H+ out of the matrix, establishing an electrochemical gradient. They do not directly transfer a phosphate to ADP. ATP synthase later uses proton return to drive ATP synthesis.

**Source:** Week 10 objectives, item 4; Lecture 10:9–10:16.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w10-lo04 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Follow energy through two transformations. Electron-transfer energy first drives proton pumping, storing energy across the membrane; proton return then drives ATP synthase. This sequence explains why the ETC and ATP synthase should not be assigned the same direct chemical task.

Trace energy conservation in two stages. First, electrons pass through the respiratory system toward oxygen. Some of the associated free-energy decrease is used by proton-pumping complexes to move H+ from matrix to intermembrane space. This stores energy in an electrochemical difference across the selective inner membrane instead of capturing it immediately as ATP.

Second, protons return toward the matrix through ATP synthase. Their return powers the coupled process that forms ATP from ADP and Pi. The distinction is crucial: electron transport builds the energy store, while ATP synthase uses it. The ETC does not directly transfer a phosphate from a substrate to ADP. This also explains uncoupling: electron flow can continue while a leak dissipates the intermediate gradient, reducing the fraction of energy ultimately conserved as ATP.

**Review:** [Week 10 study guide](../study-guides/week10-etc-oxidative-phosphorylation.qmd).
:::

### Objective W10-05 — Proton-motive force {#w10-lo05}

**Original objective:** What is the proton motive force

Define the proton-motive force and state BOTH components.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
It is the electrochemical driving force across the inner mitochondrial membrane. One component is the H+ concentration difference (chemical or pH gradient); the other is the electrical potential from charge separation. Both favor proton return toward the matrix in the respiring mitochondrion shown in the lecture.

**Source:** Week 10 objectives, item 5; Lecture 10:14.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w10-lo05 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
A proton experiences both a concentration difference and an electrical potential across the inner membrane. Both contribute to the tendency to return toward the matrix. A complete definition therefore mentions charge separation as well as the H+ concentration or pH difference.

Describe what differs across the membrane in two ways. Chemically, the intermembrane-space side has a higher H+ concentration than the matrix side in the respiratory model. Electrically, proton pumping creates charge separation, producing a membrane potential. Together these create the electrochemical driving force called the proton-motive force.

Both contributions favor proton return toward the matrix under the conditions described. Naming only a pH gradient omits the electrical component, while naming only voltage omits the concentration component. NADH oxidation is an upstream source of energy for building this force, not its definition. The force is useful because ATP synthase couples controlled proton return to its rotary and catalytic cycle. A proton leak can dissipate the force without capturing the corresponding energy in ATP.

**Review:** [Week 10 study guide](../study-guides/week10-etc-oxidative-phosphorylation.qmd).
:::

### Objective W10-06 — Proton pumps and direction {#w10-lo06}

**Original objective:** Which components of the Electron Transport Chain pump protons and what is the directionality

Identify the proton-pumping complexes, the non-pumping complex, and the directions of pumping and ATP-synthase proton return.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Complexes **I, III and IV** pump H+ **from matrix to intermembrane space**. Complex II transfers electrons but does not pump protons. During ATP synthesis, H+ returns **from intermembrane space to matrix through ATP synthase**. Distinguish electron flow along the chain from proton movement across the membrane.

**Source:** Week 10 objectives, item 6; Lecture 10:14–10:18.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w10-lo06 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Keep three distinctions visible: electron flow versus proton movement, pumping versus return, and pumping complexes versus Complex II. I, III and IV move H+ out of the matrix, while ATP synthase permits productive return. Complex II contributes electrons without adding its own pumping step.

Use two different arrow types on a diagram. Electron-flow arrows connect respiratory carriers and ultimately oxygen. Proton-pumping arrows cross the inner membrane from matrix to intermembrane space. The complexes identified as pumps are **I, III, and IV**. Complex II contributes electron transfer but lacks the proton-pumping function.

Then draw the ATP-synthase return arrow in the opposite direction, from intermembrane space back to matrix. Pumping builds the electrochemical gradient; return through ATP synthase uses it. Reversing those directions would reverse the intended energy-conservation story. The non-pumping status of Complex II also explains why its linked electron entry misses the pumping contribution of Complex I. Do not assume that being part of the ETC automatically means a component pumps protons, or that proton movement is the same physical route as electron flow along the chain.

**Review:** [Week 10 study guide](../study-guides/week10-etc-oxidative-phosphorylation.qmd).
:::

### Objective W10-07 — ATP substrates and matrix entry {#w10-lo07}

**Original objective:** What are the substrate for ATP synthesis and how do they get into the matrix

Name BOTH substrates and explain how they reach the matrix; do not stop at naming ATP synthase.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The substrates are **ADP and inorganic phosphate (Pi)**. They reach the matrix through inner-membrane transport proteins, rather than freely diffusing through the membrane. Adenine-nucleotide transport exchanges ADP into the matrix for ATP leaving it; phosphate is transported in by a phosphate transport system. ATP synthase then uses matrix-side ADP and Pi. The lecture's required general answer is “through transport proteins”; carrier names are supporting detail, not an extra memorization requirement.

**Source:** Week 10 objectives, item 7; Lecture 10:20; Alberts Ch. 14.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w10-lo07 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The selective inner membrane makes substrate supply a separate problem from catalysis. ADP and Pi need transport systems to reach the matrix-side catalytic machinery, and ATP must be exported. Explaining this access completes the answer even without memorizing extra transporter names.

Distinguish three tasks: delivering substrates, forming ATP, and exporting product. The immediate substrates are ADP and inorganic phosphate. Because the inner membrane is selective, each needs transport-dependent access to the matrix side rather than unrestricted diffusion. Adenine-nucleotide transport brings ADP in while ATP leaves, and a phosphate-transport system supplies Pi.

ATP synthase then uses the available matrix-side ADP and Pi, with proton return providing the driving mechanism. NADH and oxygen participate upstream in respiration but are not the pair of chemical substrates joined at its catalytic site. Naming ATP synthase alone therefore leaves the entry part of the question unanswered. The course requires the general idea of transport proteins; the carrier descriptions support that reasoning without creating an additional memorization requirement beyond the stated objective.

**Review:** [Week 10 study guide](../study-guides/week10-etc-oxidative-phosphorylation.qmd).
:::

### Objective W10-08 — ATP synthase conformations {#w10-lo08}

**Original objective:** What happens in each of the three conformations of the alpha-beta dimers of ATP synthase

State the role of Loose, Tight and Open and explain how proton movement changes the stationary dimers.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Loose:** ADP and Pi enter and are held. **Tight:** ATP is formed. **Open:** ATP is released. Proton flow through the membrane Fo region drives the rotor and central γ shaft. The three αβ dimers remain stationary but change conformation as γ turns, so each catalytic site progresses through the states. Do not say the αβ head rotates as one rigid wheel.

**Source:** Week 10 objectives, item 8; Lecture 10:21–10:24; Tutorial 6.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w10-lo08 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Follow one catalytic site through Loose, Tight and Open: substrate binding, ATP formation and release. Proton-driven shaft rotation forces these shape changes in stationary catalytic units. The important connection is movement producing altered binding and catalytic states, not rotation of the head as a whole.

Follow one catalytic site through its functional sequence. In the **loose** state, ADP and Pi are held. In the **tight** state, ATP formation is favored. In the **open** state, ATP can be released. These are changes in the catalytic site's conformation, not three separate enzymes that pass ATP between unrelated compartments.

Explain what drives the changes. Proton flow through the membrane-associated F0 machinery turns the rotor and central γ shaft. The αβ units remain positioned in the catalytic head but change shape as the shaft's orientation changes. Thus stationary does not mean chemically inactive, and rotation does not mean the whole head spins as a rigid wheel. The binding-change sequence connects proton return, mechanical motion, and ATP output. Release from a catalytic site is also distinct from subsequent transport of ATP across the inner membrane.

**Review:** [Week 10 study guide](../study-guides/week10-etc-oxidative-phosphorylation.qmd).
:::

### Objective W10-09 — Thermogenin {#w10-lo09}

**Original objective:** What is thermogenin

Identify thermogenin, its location and its effects on proton return, ATP yield and heat.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Thermogenin (UCP1) is an uncoupling protein in the inner mitochondrial membrane of brown-adipose mitochondria. It permits proton return toward the matrix without driving ATP synthase. Consequently less gradient energy is captured in ATP and more is dissipated as heat. Fuel oxidation and electron transport can continue; thermogenin is not simply an ETC inhibitor.

**Source:** Week 10 objectives, item 9; Lecture 10, thermogenin slides; Tutorial 6.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w10-lo09 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
UCP1 provides a bypass across the same membrane used to store proton-gradient energy. Protons can return without ATP-synthase capture, shifting energy toward heat. That explains brown-fat thermogenesis while distinguishing uncoupling from simply blocking the respiratory chain.

Identify the protein and then explain why its location matters. Thermogenin, or UCP1, is in the inner mitochondrial membrane of brown-adipose mitochondria, where it can provide a proton-return route across the same membrane that holds the respiratory gradient. Protons can return toward the matrix without passing through the ATP-synthase route that captures their energy as ATP.

The consequence is a change in energy partition: less ATP is captured per fuel oxidized and more energy is dispersed as heat. This is why brown fat can support heat production while still using fuel and oxygen. Do not define thermogenin as a complete ETC blocker; the key is the bypass between gradient formation and ATP synthesis. Likewise, it does not raise ATP output by preventing proton movement. Its function depends on permitting a different route for that movement.

**Review:** [Week 10 study guide](../study-guides/week10-etc-oxidative-phosphorylation.qmd).
:::

# Part C — Integrated Practice

### Integrated Question 1 — Oxygen removal
Predict what happens to electron flow, proton pumping, and ATP synthesis if oxygen is suddenly removed.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Without oxygen as the final electron acceptor, electron flow through the ETC backs up, proton pumping declines, the proton-motive force collapses, and oxidative ATP synthesis falls sharply.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w10-ix01 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Oxygen is the final outlet for electrons, so removing it causes the upstream chain to back up. Without sustained electron flow, proton pumping cannot maintain the gradient. As the stored driving force dissipates, oxidative ATP production falls; the question concerns that respiratory source of ATP.

Reason from the terminal step backward, then follow the energy consequences forward. Oxygen is the final electron acceptor. When it is removed, terminal transfer cannot continue normally, so upstream carriers increasingly lack a way to pass their electrons onward. Sustained electron flow therefore declines, and the pumping driven by that flow cannot be maintained.

As existing gradient energy is used or dissipated without adequate replenishment, the proton-motive force falls. ATP synthase then loses the driving force for oxidative ATP production. The decline need not mean that every previously established gradient disappears instantaneously at the moment oxygen is removed; the prediction concerns loss of sustained operation. Also distinguish oxidative ATP synthesis from all ATP production in the cell: the question targets the respiratory system, not a claim that glycolytic substrate-level phosphorylation is directly oxygen-dependent. The full causal chain is terminal acceptor loss, backed-up electron flow, reduced pumping, falling gradient, and sharply reduced oxidative ATP output.

**Review:** [Week 10 study guide](../study-guides/week10-etc-oxidative-phosphorylation.qmd).
:::

### Integrated Question 2 — Complex II mutation
A mutation prevents Complex II from transferring electrons but leaves I, III, and IV normal. Which electron source is most directly impaired?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Electron entry associated with **FADH2/succinate oxidation** is most directly impaired because Complex II is the entry point for those electrons.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w10-ix02 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Locate the lesion at the electron-entry step. Complex II transfers the electrons associated with succinate oxidation and its bound flavin, so that route is directly impaired. Normal Complex I activity does not repair a blockage specifically at Complex II.

Locate the lesion at the entry route specified by the question. Complex II supplies electron entry associated with succinate oxidation and FAD-linked transfer in the CAC/ETC connection. Preventing its electron transfer most directly impairs that source of electrons. It does not mean Complex II has lost a proton-pumping function, because it is not a pump in the normal system either.

The question explicitly leaves Complexes I, III, and IV normal. NADH-linked entry through Complex I therefore is not the component directly disabled by the mutation. The available information supports a source-specific prediction, not an exact numerical ATP yield or a claim that all respiratory electron transfer must cease. Distinguish the location of electron entry from the later common pathway and the proton pumps. This makes the answer precise about the direct defect without inventing measurements of the whole cell's remaining metabolism.

**Review:** [Week 10 study guide](../study-guides/week10-etc-oxidative-phosphorylation.qmd).
:::

### Integrated Question 3 — Inner membrane leak
Why would a proton-leaky inner membrane decrease ATP production even if NADH oxidation continues?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The leak dissipates the proton-motive force. Electron transport can still release energy and pump protons, but the stored gradient cannot build sufficiently to power ATP synthase efficiently.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w10-ix03 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Continued NADH oxidation alone does not guarantee efficient ATP production. A leaky membrane lets pumped protons return by routes that do not drive ATP synthase, preventing effective energy storage. The defect breaks the gradient-mediated coupling between the two processes.

A working proton pump is useful for ATP production only if the membrane can retain enough of the gradient it builds. In the leaky membrane, protons return through an alternative route instead of all being directed through ATP synthase. NADH oxidation can still release energy and support pumping, but the leak dissipates the electrochemical difference before as much of that energy can be captured in ATP.

This separates failure of coupling from failure of electron donation. The observation that NADH oxidation continues rules out an explanation based simply on all electron flow having stopped. The defect lies in conserving and using the intermediate proton gradient. More energy is dissipated without ATP-synthase capture, including as heat, so ATP yield falls. The question does not supply a leak size or quantitative rate, so the conclusion is directional rather than a numerical prediction. State the gradient loss and bypass mechanism, not only that the membrane is damaged.

**Review:** [Week 10 study guide](../study-guides/week10-etc-oxidative-phosphorylation.qmd).
:::

### Integrated Question 4 — Brown fat
Explain why brown adipose tissue can consume fuel and oxygen while generating relatively less ATP and more heat.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Thermogenin allows protons to bypass ATP synthase. Electron transport and proton pumping continue, but gradient energy is dissipated as heat instead of being efficiently captured in ATP.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w10-ix04 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Fuel and oxygen consumption can continue while ATP yield falls because energy need not end up in ATP. UCP1 gives protons a bypass, so more gradient energy becomes heat. The tissue's thermogenic role follows from this deliberately uncoupled energy partition.

Compare brown-fat mitochondria with the fully coupled arrangement. In both, fuel oxidation can supply reduced carriers, electrons can pass toward oxygen, and respiratory complexes can pump protons. In brown fat with thermogenin active, an additional route allows protons to return toward the matrix without driving ATP synthase. That route changes what happens to the energy stored in the gradient.

A smaller share is captured in ATP and a larger share is dissipated as heat. Fuel and oxygen consumption are therefore compatible with relatively low ATP capture; they do not prove that every unit of respiratory energy must become ATP. The explanation should not say that thermogenin simply blocks all electron transport or that heat is produced because no fuel is oxidized. Its role is specifically to uncouple part of the proton-return process from ATP synthesis. This is the mechanism linking brown-adipose mitochondrial structure and UCP1 activity to thermogenesis in the course example.

**Review:** [Week 10 study guide](../study-guides/week10-etc-oxidative-phosphorylation.qmd).
:::

### Integrated Question 5 — ETC versus ATP synthase
In one sentence, distinguish the jobs of the ETC and ATP synthase.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The ETC uses electron-transfer energy to build a proton gradient, whereas ATP synthase uses the energy stored in that gradient to make ATP from ADP and Pi.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w10-ix05 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Assign one energy-conversion job to each system. The ETC converts electron-transfer energy into a proton gradient; ATP synthase converts that gradient's energy into ATP. Keeping the jobs separate explains both normal coupling and the consequences of a proton leak.

The two systems are linked by a shared intermediate energy store, not by identical chemistry. The ETC transfers electrons toward oxygen and uses part of the released energy to pump H+ across the inner membrane. ATP synthase does not take over that electron-transfer job. It uses the return of protons down the electrochemical gradient to drive its rotary catalytic mechanism and form ATP from ADP and Pi.

A good one-sentence response can therefore use the contrast **builds the gradient** versus **uses the gradient**. That wording explains why the two are functionally coupled but experimentally separable. A proton leak, for example, can allow ongoing electron transport while reducing ATP capture, because it interrupts the useful intermediate energy store rather than removing every electron-transfer reaction. Avoid saying the ETC directly phosphorylates ADP or that ATP synthase's chemical substrates are NADH and FADH2. Those statements erase the very division of labor the question asks you to explain.

**Review:** [Week 10 study guide](../study-guides/week10-etc-oxidative-phosphorylation.qmd).
:::
